title: Two-Dimensional Kinematics
learning_objectives: Add and subtract vectors graphically and analytically, and use the result for velocity.
Analyse projectile motion: the horizontal and the vertical motion handled separately.
Work out the range, the maximum height and the time of flight of a projectile.

sections.title: Introduction to Two-Dimensional Kinematics
objectives: Describe what changes when motion is no longer along a straight line.

misconceptions.claim: Motion in two dimensions is just motion in one dimension done twice.
misconceptions.correction: Two dimensional motion is described by two coordinates, and the two of them follow separate rules.

summary: Two dimensional motion needs two coordinates, usually x and y.
The horizontal and the vertical motion are handled separately.
The reason is that gravity acts only in the vertical direction.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Kinematics in Two Dimensions: An Introduction
objectives: State that the x and the y coordinates are independent of each other.
Explain why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile can be analysed separately.

misconceptions.claim: A ball thrown into the air travels in a curve because it is pushed sideways by the air.
misconceptions.correction: The curve comes from the two motions acting at once. The horizontal motion is steady, and the vertical motion is accelerated by gravity.

summary: The x and the y motions are independent.
Each one follows the rules of one dimensional motion.
The path of the object is the curve that the two together describe.

authored_exercises.stem: A ball is launched horizontally from a cliff. Neglecting air resistance, which force acts on the ball after launch?
authored_exercises.answer: Only its weight, the downward force of gravity.
solution: After launch, the hand no longer touches the ball.
The only force is gravity, which acts vertically downward.
No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity stays constant.

authored_exercises.stem: A projectile moves horizontally at a constant 8 m/s. How far does it travel horizontally in 3 s?
solution: The horizontal velocity is constant at 8 m/s.

authored_exercises.stem: A package is released from a plane flying horizontally. Ignoring air resistance, does the package land directly below the release point? Explain.
authored_exercises.answer: No. It keeps the plane’s horizontal velocity, so it lands ahead of the release point.
solution: At release, the package already has the plane’s horizontal velocity.
No horizontal force acts on it, so that velocity persists.
It therefore moves forward while falling and lands ahead of the point below the release.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on Kinematics in Two Dimensions: An Introduction has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Graphical Methods
objectives: Add two vectors by drawing them head to tail and measuring the resultant.
Subtract a vector by adding its reverse.

misconceptions.claim: To subtract a vector, draw it again pointing the other way and add it.
misconceptions.correction: That is exactly right. The reverse of a vector has the same size and the opposite direction, so adding it is the subtraction.

misconceptions.claim: Vectors are added by adding their magnitudes.
misconceptions.correction: Vectors are added as arrows, head to tail, and the resultant is the diagonal.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-2, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the sum of the magnitudes as an option.

summary: A vector is drawn as an arrow, with the tail at the starting point.
Vectors add head to tail, and the resultant runs from the first tail to the last head.

sections.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Analytical Methods
objectives: Resolve a vector into components and add the components separately.
Calculate the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector from its components.

misconceptions.claim: You have to add vectors by drawing them, there is no other way.
misconceptions.correction: Drawing works, but for numbers it is slow and imprecise. Resolving into components gives the same answer exactly.

misconceptions.claim: The components of a vector are found by adding it up and dividing.
misconceptions.correction: The components are the projections of the vector on the axes, and the magnitude follows from them.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the sum of the components as an option.

summary: A vector can be broken into components along chosen axes.
The components are added one axis at a time, and then put back together.
The magnitude and the direction of the resultant follow from its components.

sections.title: Projectile Motion
objectives: Analyse a projectile by splitting its motion into horizontal and vertical parts.
Calculate the time of flight, the maximum height and the range of a projectile.

misconceptions.claim: The projectile keeps the speed it was launched with for the whole flight.
misconceptions.correction: The horizontal speed stays the same, because there is no horizontal force. The vertical speed changes every second, because gravity acts downward.

summary: The horizontal motion is uniform, the vertical motion is accelerated.
The time of flight is set by the vertical motion alone.
The maximum height is reached when the vertical velocity is zero.

sections.title: Addition of Velocities
objectives: Add the velocities of a moving frame and of an object to find the velocity seen by an observer.
Apply vector addition to relative velocity.

misconceptions.claim: If you run twice as fast on a moving train, you move twice as fast compared with the ground.
misconceptions.correction: Your speed compared with the train is unchanged, but compared with the ground the two velocities add.

misconceptions.claim: The velocity an observer sees is the velocity of the object alone.
misconceptions.correction: It is the sum of the object's velocity and the velocity of the frame the observer is in.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the velocity of the frame as an option.

summary: The velocity an observer measures is the sum of the object's velocity and the velocity of the frame.
The sum is a vector sum, so directions matter.
The same reasoning gives the relative velocity of two objects.

conditions.text: For motion in a plane, with the axes chosen for the problem.

sec-3:exr-113.stem: Suppose you first walk 12.0 m in a direction $20º$ west of north and then 20.0 m in a direction $40.0º$ south of west. How far are you from your starting point, and what is the compass direction of a line connecting your starting point to your final position? (If you represent the two legs of the walk as vector displacements $A$ and $B$ , then this problem finds their sum $R = A + B$ .)

sec-6:exr-87.stem: (a) Another airplane is flying in a jet stream that is blowing at 45.0 m/s in a direction $20º$ south of east. Its direction of motion relative to the Earth is $45.0º$ south of west, while its direction of travel relative to the air is $5.00º$ south of west. What is the airplane’s speed relative to the air mass? (b) What is the airplane’s speed relative to the Earth?

sec-6:exr-98.stem: Five galaxies lie along a straight line at distances of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Mly from the Milky Way. Their recession velocities are 1490, 2980, 4470, 5960, and 7450 km/s, respectively. (a) Find the rate of expansion (the Hubble constant) as a function of distance. (b) If you extrapolate back in time, how long ago were all of the galaxies at approximately the same position?
solution: For each galaxy, divide the recession velocity by its distance: $H=v/d$. Every pair gives the same value, $H=14.9\ \mathrm{km/s}$ per Mly, so the expansion rate is uniform.
If the galaxies have always moved apart at this rate, the time since they were together is $t=1/H$.
Convert to years: $t=(6.35\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{s})/(3.16\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s/y})=2.0\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{y}$, about 20 billion years.
sec-6:exr-98.solution_provenance: adapted from the OpenStax CNXML exercise, with the source figure's data written into the stem

sec-5:exr-86.stem: A projectile is launched at ground level at $45^{\circ}$ with initial speeds of 30, 40, and 50 m/s. Calculate the range for each launch and verify that the ranges are proportional to the square of the initial speed.
solution: The range on level ground is $R=v_{0}^{2}\sin(2\theta)/g$. For $\theta=45^{\circ}$, $\sin(2\theta)=1$, so $R=v_{0}^{2}/g$.
Each range equals $v_{0}^{2}/g$, so the range is proportional to $v_{0}^{2}$.
